title: Açaí: what it is and what nutrients it contains

seo.title: Açaí: what it is and its nutrition profile
seo.meta_description: Açaí pulp is unusual for a fruit: relatively high in fat, low in sugar and rich in dark pigments. See how frozen pulp, powder and bowls differ.
seo.search_intent: Understand what açaí is and what its natural nutrition profile looks like

excerpt: Açaí is the fruit of Amazonian Euterpe palms. Its pulp is unusual among fruits because much of its energy comes from fat rather than sugar, and it can provide fiber and anthocyanins. Frozen purée, freeze-dried powder, drinks and bowls are not nutritionally interchangeable because water, added sugar and toppings change the numbers dramatically.
content_html:
Açaí did not begin as purple powder or a granola-topped bowl. It is a small dark fruit from Amazonian palms, especially Euterpe oleracea, and its edible pulp is processed soon after harvest.

Its nutrition profile has one striking feature: açaí pulp is naturally much fattier and less sugary than the stereotype of a sweet berry.

What does the pulp contain?

Water content varies with processing, so there is no single universal number for every purée. A current U.S. unsweetened frozen product provides 70 calories, 5 g fat, 3 g fiber, 1 g protein and 0 g total sugar per 100 g packet.

Freeze-drying shows how much water controls concentration. One analyzed dry sample contained roughly 49.1 g fat, 20.3 g fiber, 9.2 g protein and 2.7 g total sugars per 100 g dry matter. Those numbers should not be transferred directly to hydrated frozen pulp.

Why is açaí relatively high in fat?

Oleic acid is prominent in its lipid fraction, along with palmitic and linoleic acids. That helps explain why açaí behaves differently from strawberries or blueberries, which contain very little fat.

The dry-matter figure does not mean a frozen packet is 50% fat. The current 100 g packet above contains 5 g—water has changed the concentration enormously.

Fiber depends on keeping the pulp

The same unsweetened frozen packet lists 3 g fiber per 100 g. A filtered drink or juice may retain far less, while a freeze-dried powder concentrates the solids.

That is why ‘açaí’ on the front of a package is not enough information. The form matters.

The purple color comes from anthocyanins

Açaí contains dark pigments including cyanidin derivatives. These compounds are scientifically interesting, but an antioxidant assay is not proof that one serving treats or prevents disease.

Frozen pulp, powder and bowls are different foods in practice

Water dilutes nutrients per 100 g; drying concentrates them; added sweeteners and toppings can raise carbohydrate and calorie content. When buying açaí, check the ingredient list, added sugars, fiber and serving size.

The fruit has a distinctive composition. The nutrition of the product you eat depends on what happened after the fruit was harvested.

faq.question: Is açaí naturally high in sugar?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Natural pulp is relatively low in sugar compared with many fruits; the current unsweetened frozen example lists 0 g total sugar per 100 g.

faq.question: Why does açaí contain more fat than most berries?
faq.answer: The pulp naturally contains lipids, with oleic acid prominent in the fatty-acid profile.

faq.question: Does açaí have fiber?
faq.answer: Yes when the pulp solids are retained. The current unsweetened frozen example provides 3 g fiber per 100 g.

faq.question: Is açaí powder the same as frozen pulp?
faq.answer: No. Powder has lost much of its water, so fat, fiber and other solids are much more concentrated by weight.
